title: Speak sweetly
hook: speak insipid words and body and mind grow insipid (Asa di Var, ang 473)

segments.voice: Yesterday, eyes and ears, and your line: clean eyes, clean ears. Did you step away from a rumor? Today the var comes back to the tongue, but from the kitchen this time. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

Taste a spoonful of dal before the salt goes in. It isn't bad, exactly. It isn't poisoned or burned. It's just flat. Lifeless. You take one bite and push the bowl away. Punjabi has a word for that taste: fikka. Tea without sugar is fikka. A party where nobody talks is fikka. And Guru Nanak used the same kitchen word, in a salok of the Asa di Var, for a certain kind of speech. Not lying, which we met two days ago. Something more ordinary, and maybe more common.
screen: `DAL BEFORE THE SALT.` → `FIKKA: FLAT, TASTELESS.` → `A KITCHEN WORD FOR SPEECH.`

segments.voice: The salok is on ang 473. In paraphrase: speaking fikka words, the body and mind become fikka. The fikka person is called fikka; the fikka person gets a fikka name. The fikka are cast out of the Court of the Lord, and get slapped in the face for it. The fikka are called fools, and are punished with shoes. The word repeats until you can taste it. Fikka here means insipid, but it also leans toward harsh, rude, sour: words with no sweetness and no care in them. A curt reply. A sarcastic dig. A cold one-word answer to someone who needed more. Here's the claim that surprises people. The salok doesn't only say fikka words hurt the listener. It says they make the speaker fikka. Body and mind. Speak flat and sour long enough, and you become flat and sour. Your reputation follows: people start to call you that. Anyone who's watched a person harden over the years has seen this happen. Words aren't just output. They're practice. Every sentence trains the one who says it. This connects back to mitthat neevee from day five hundred fifty-one: sweetness and humility as the essence of virtue. That was about who you are. Today is about how you get there. Sweet speech isn't flattery or fake niceness. It means words with some care cooked into them. Salt in the dal. Sugar in the tea. Something that makes the other person want to stay at the table.
screen: `FIKKA: FLAT, HARSH, SOUR.` · `FIKKA WORDS MAKE A FIKKA PERSON.` · `EVERY SENTENCE IS PRACTICE.` · `CARE COOKED INTO WORDS.` · then, large: `SWEET WORDS, SWEET LIFE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say something warm. Sit and breathe. Think of the last flat or sharp thing you said to someone, maybe today, maybe yesterday. Don't scold yourself. Just hear it again. Now imagine saying it with care cooked in: the same truth, a warmer sentence. Then think of someone who'd be glad to hear something kind from you. Find the words now: simple, true, warm. Hold them ready. If you pray, you can say Waheguru first. The bell holds the time.
Speak sweetly. Guru Nanak's warning about fikka words, flat and harsh like dal without salt: they make the body and mind of the speaker fikka too.
Your line: sweet words, sweet life. Today, say your warm words out loud to that person, by phone, in a message, or face to face. Day five hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Sikhs hear this salok on fikka speech in the dawn singing of Asa di Var, and sweet, humble speech is counted among the marks of a Sikh's character.

original.note: Gurmukhi: fikka, insipid, tasteless, harsh; an everyday kitchen word Guru Nanak uses for speech.

trapdoor: what it means: flat, harsh words make the speaker flat and harsh; sweet words, with care in them, shape a sweet life.
what a scholar hears: the salok repeats fikka in nearly every phrase, so the sound itself turns sour; it pairs with mitthat neevee earlier in the var.
